newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Police investigate mines planted on Papal route.
newsitem.headline: Police investigate mines planted on Papal route.

text.p: Bosnian security forces questioned 20 people but have not yet charged anyone in connection with explosives planted along the route taken by Pope John Paul II in Sarajevo, police said on Tuesday.
Police dismantled 23 anti-tank mines and plastic explosives last Saturday under a main boulevard shortly before the Pope arrived in Sarajevo.
Authorities were investigating "two groups" as possible perpetrators, Mehmed Zilic, Moslem-Croat federation interior minister, told a news conference.
Zilic said he could not give details.
"This must have been done by special (military) forces because very few people can handle such devices," he said.
The mines were connected to a detonator and a remote control walkie-talkie, allowing the explosives to be detonated at a distance of up to 1,000 metres (yards), Zilic said.
Zilic said the interior ministry had not ruled out the possibility that the bombing of a Roman Catholic church in Sarajevo last month may have been linked to the explosives found on Saturday.
The bomb that detonated at the back door of the church on March 4 had a clock mechanism, Zilic said.

Authorities found the explosives after receiving a tip from a guard at a nearby building. The guard reported seeing a man in boots with a shovel walking away from the bridge on Mesa Selimovic boulevard.
"We suspect that this person spotted was connecting the mines and setting up the detonator," Zilic said.
Police had also found footprints from an army boot, he said.
The interior ministry insisted its security precautions for the Papal trip had proved effective and rejected criticism from U.N. police monitors.
A spokesman for the United Nations mission said on Monday that it was "extremely worrying" that local police had failed to detect the explosives through its own security measures.
